Idaho Falls|United States of America.f: The town was renamed Idaho Falls in 1891 when marketers talked leaders into naming it for the rapids below the bridge.

Sioux City|United States of America.f: Sergeant Charles Floyd died at Sioux City in 1804, the only death of the two and a half year Lewis and Clark expedition.

Alpena|United States of America.f: Offshore lies Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary, which protects an estimated 116 historically significant shipwrecks.

Fargo|United States of America.f: Lenient divorce laws made Fargo the divorce capital of the Midwest during the 1880s.

Butte|United States of America.f: As of 2017, Butte has the largest population of Irish Americans per capita of any U.S. city.

Vail|United States of America.f: Vail's founder Pete Seibert served in the Army's 10th Mountain Division, which trained at Camp Hale, 14 miles south of town.

Sioux Falls|United States of America.f: In 1981 Citibank moved its main credit card center from New York City to Sioux Falls to use relaxed state usury laws.

Helena|United States of America.f: By 1888 about 50 millionaires lived in Helena, more per capita than in any city in the world.

Grand Canyon|United States of America.f: Grand Canyon Village was one of the earliest planned communities to face houses onto shared space with cars at the rear.

King Salmon|United States of America.f: King Salmon is the nearest town to Katmai National Park, home to an estimated 2,200 brown bears, the largest protected population.

Fayetteville (AR)|United States of Ameri.f: Fayetteville was named by county seat commissioners from Fayetteville, Tennessee, which was itself named for Fayetteville, North Carolina.

Flagstaff|United States of America.f: In 2001 Flagstaff was recognized by the International Dark-Sky Association as the world's first International Dark-Sky City.

Medford|United States of America.f: Medford was named in 1883 by railroad engineer David Loring after Medford, Massachusetts, near his hometown of Concord.

Bismarck|United States of America.f: Bismarck is the only U.S. state capital named for a foreign statesman, renamed in 1873 to attract German settlers and investment.

Laredo|United States of America.f: In 1840 Laredo was the capital of the independent Republic of the Rio Grande, earning it the title City Under Seven Flags.

La Crosse|United States of America.f: La Crosse is named for a stick game played there by Native Americans, whose sticks resembled a bishop's crozier, or la crosse in French.

Twin Falls|United States of America.f: Shoshone Falls near Twin Falls drops 213 feet, which is 46 feet higher than Niagara Falls.

Rapid City|United States of America.f: In 1930 the Rapid City Chamber of Commerce wrote to Al Capone inviting him to live in the Black Hills.

Green Bay|United States of America.f: Green Bay was once known as the Toilet Paper Capital of the World because of its large paper industry.

Cedar City|United States of America.f: Cedar City is named for its abundant local trees, which are actually junipers and not cedars.

Provo|United States of America.f: Fort Utah was renamed Provo in 1850 for Etienne Provost, a French-Canadian trapper who reached the region in 1825.

Columbia (SC)|United States of America.f: Columbia was laid out as one of the first planned U.S. cities, five years before L'Enfant's plan for Washington, D.C.

Cedar Rapids|United States of America.f: Cedar Rapids is home to the Mother Mosque of America, dedicated in 1934 and the longest-standing mosque in North America.

Lawton|United States of America.f: Lawton is named for Major General Henry W. Lawton, a Fort Sill quartermaster who took part in the capture of Geronimo.

Alamosa|United States of America.f: Alamosa takes its Spanish name, meaning of cottonwood, from the cottonwood forests along the Rio Grande.

Lansing|United States of America.f: Unlike every other state capital located in a county, Lansing is not a county seat, since Ingham County's seat is Mason.

Laramie|United States of America.f: Louisa Swain of Laramie became the first woman in the United States to cast a legal vote in a general election, in 1870.

Mobile|United States of America.f: Mobile was home to the first organized Carnival mystic society to hold a parade in the United States, starting in 1830.

Dothan|United States of America.f: About a fourth of the U.S. peanut crop is grown near Dothan, which is known as the Peanut Capital of the World.

Jackson (MS)|United States of America.f: Jackson sits above an extinct volcano buried 2,900 feet underground, a feature no other U.S. capital city has.

Lakeland|United States of America.f: Florida Southern College in Lakeland has the largest single-site collection of Frank Lloyd Wright buildings in the world.

Decatur (IL)|United States of America.f: Decatur was the original home of the Chicago Bears, who played there as the Decatur Staleys in 1919 and 1920.

Erie|United States of America.f: On December 24 and 25, 2017, Erie got 53 inches of snow, the largest two-day snowfall anywhere in Pennsylvania.

South Bend|United States of America.f: South Bend has the nation's only ballpark synagogue, built in 1901 on the grounds of the South Bend Cubs stadium.

West Yellowstone|United States of Americ.f: West Yellowstone holds the lowest temperature ever recorded in a residential community in the contiguous U.S., at -66 F.

Waterloo|United States of America.f: The Waterloo Hawks were a founding member of the NBA but folded after a single season in 1949-50.

Santa Fe|United States of America.f: Founded in 1610, Santa Fe is the oldest U.S. state capital and, at 7,199 feet above sea level, also the highest.

Shreveport|United States of America.f: A yellow fever epidemic in 1873 killed 759 Shreveport residents in just 80 days.

Tyler|United States of America.f: The Adopt-a-Highway movement began in Tyler in 1985, when a local Civitan chapter adopted a stretch of road.

Burlington (VT)|United States of America.f: The world's first lake-going steamboat was built in Burlington in 1808.
